name: N-acetylcysteine (NAC)
summary: N-acetylcysteine (NAC), also called acetylcysteine, is a modified form of the amino acid cysteine. It is both a medicine with specific medical uses and an ingredient sold in supplements; those uses and products should not be confused.
commonUses: Used in supplements marketed for antioxidant support
Used in supplements marketed for glutathione support
roles: NAC supplies cysteine, a building block for the body's glutathione.
Its chemical action on bonds in mucus proteins underlies its use in mucus-thinning medicines; this is not a general supplement benefit claim.

status.note: This basic guide does not provide a routine status test. It does not define an NAC deficiency.

high.note: See the cautions below; this guide does not establish a safe upper amount.

forms.name: Oral supplements
forms.note: Capsules and powders are sold as supplements. Their marketing is separate from the indications and supervision attached to medicines.

forms.name: Acetylcysteine medicines
forms.note: Medical formulations include oral, inhaled and intravenous products. Route and purpose matter; an oral supplement is not a substitute for emergency or prescribed treatment.

reference.noUpperLimit: This basic guide does not provide reference intakes or upper-limit values.

interactions.note: NAC can increase the blood-pressure-lowering effect of nitroglycerin. Discuss the combination with the prescribing clinician or pharmacist.

cautions: Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea can occur with NAC.
Acetylcysteine is used medically for paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning. Suspected poisoning needs urgent medical care, not self-treatment with a supplement.
Safety information for an intravenous or inhaled medicine cannot simply be applied to an oral supplement. This guide does not establish long-term supplement safety.

sources.title: N-Acetylcysteine: A Review of Clinical Usefulness (an Old Drug with New Tricks).
